newsitem.title: GERMANY: F.O. LICHT - Daily coffee report.
newsitem.headline: F.O. LICHT - Daily coffee report.

text.p: The following is a direct contribution from statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

COFFEE: World market for September 13 - Robusta futures in London closed firmer across the board in light trade as a strong arabicas performance encouraged industry bargain-hunting to drag values off their earlier lows. November added $13 to close at $1,534.

In New York arabica futures closed mixed after the market capitulated late in the day to persistent origin selling. However, prompt supplies of mild coffees are still tight, underpinning spot differentials.

Spreads for forward delivery eased ahead of the upcoming Colombian and Central American harvests. September added 40 points to close at 115.25 cents/lb while December shed 50 points to close at 104.70 cents/lb.

COLOMBIA - Colombia will put up for October/November sale around 260,000 kg-bags of coffee from its December export quota because of end-of-the year harvest uncertainties, the National Coffee Federation commercial vice president John Naranjo said. The federation predicts at least a 30 per cent drop in the original estimate of an October/December harvest of 8 million bags.

The end-of-the year harvest usually represents about 60 per cent of the entire annual crop, trade sources said. The extra coffee will be made available to private exporters and not the federation, Naranjo added. Thus private exporters will have 1.4 million bags to sell over the next two months, according to Naranjo.
Under the ACPC retention scheme, Colombia has an October/December quota of 3.05 million bags, which is expected to be exported in three even monthly quotas of 1.017 million bags.
Naranjo said the federation does not at this moment plan to offer any of the national coffee fund stocks to private exporters despite the anticipated scarcity.

However, he emphasized that Colombia still has around 5 million bags of exportable coffee in stock. But private exporters eschewed an offer of 100,000 bags of Fund stocks to meet deliveries last month because of additional transport costs and because some traders fear the coffee is of lower quality than freshly harvested beans.

BRAZIL - On September 12, The Brazilian senate approved a bill making exports of primary commodities in some semi-manufactured goods exempt from the so-called ICMS export tax. The bill is expected to take effect September 16 after president Hernando Henrique Cardoso signs the law.
The Planning Ministry estimates exports to grow between 6 and 12 per cent as a result of the measure. It noted the impact on exports would be the equivalent of a seven per cent devaluation.

INDIA - India has freed the coffee trade by changing a 50 year-old law that allows the state-run Coffee Board to handle a bulk of the trade. Under previous rules large growers were obliged to send the board 30 per cent of their harvest and only small growers were allowed a 100 per cent free-sale quota.

Now also large growers are no longer forced to sell 30 per cent of their output to the Coffee Board. This means that the free-sale quota is now 100 per cent. The Coffee Board will now concentrate on research and development as well as helping Indian exporters to develop the international market for Indian coffee.

BRAZIL - Brazil exported 2.566 million bags of coffee in April/June 1996, which compares to 3.967 million bags exported the same period in 1995. Total exports in crop year 1995/96 (April/March) reached 13.655 million bags up from 15.837 million bags exported the previous year.

Major countries of destination for green coffee in April/June 1996 were Italy (290,100 vs 489,000 bags), the United States (213,300 vs 611,900 bags) and Japan (227,000 vs 304,800 bags). The main market for solubles remained Russia with 166,200 bags in April/June 1996, down from 244,700 bags the same period in 1995. The second largest market were the United States with 173,800 bags vs 99,400 bags.
